explanations.explanation: Three months, baker. The text says, “After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island.” (Acts 28:11) That's a long stretch on one island. The ship they boarded had spent the winter there too.

Close, but the text says months, not weeks. “After three months we set sail…” (Acts 28:11). Three weeks is barely enough time to find where they keep the spoons. Think of it as a much bigger stay than that.
A full YEAR, friend? That's four times too long! The text says, “After three months we set sail…” (Acts 28:11). Even my slowest batch is out of the oven and cooling before a year is up.

explanations.answer: Invite the group to stay with them
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says they found brothers “who invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) Fellow believers, and the first thing they do is open the door. A good host is a gift, friend.

explanations.answer: Send the group straight on to Rome
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets shooed down the road here. The brothers invited the group to spend the week with them, and only after that does the text say, “And so we came to Rome.” (Acts 28:14) The stop in Puteoli came first. A week of rest and company before the last stretch sounds good to me.

explanations.answer: Report the group to the soldiers
explanations.explanation: No reporting here, baker. These were brothers, fellow believers in Jesus, and what they did was invite the group to spend the week with them (Acts 28:14). Nothing in the text has them talking to the soldiers at all. It's a welcome, not a tattle.
A week it is. The text says the brothers “invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) Seven days of company before the road to Rome. I'd take that kind of invitation any day.

A month would be a big stay, but the text says week. “…invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) Their stay in Puteoli was shorter than you picked. A month is more like what they spent on Malta.
A year! Those brothers would need a LOT of extra pillows. The text says, “…invited us to spend the week with them.” (Acts 28:14) One week, and then they came to Rome.

True. “When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.” (Acts 28:15) The believers had heard about the group and traveled out to meet them. Paul saw friendly faces on the road, and he thanked God right there. I think seeing them did him a world of good.

It's true, friend. The text says, “When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.” (Acts 28:15) The believers from Rome had traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet the group. Paul saw them, and he was encouraged. Then he gave thanks to God.

explanations.answer: By himself with a soldier to guard him
explanations.explanation: That's it. “…Paul was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.” (Acts 28:16) He's still a prisoner, but he gets his own place with a soldier watching him. I think that's a lot better than what I expected for a prisoner.

explanations.answer: In the city prison with other prisoners
explanations.explanation: Not the city prison, baker. The text says Paul “was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.” (Acts 28:16) By himself, so no crowded cell. A soldier does guard him, though, so he's still a prisoner.

explanations.answer: In the house of a Roman official
explanations.explanation: No Roman official's house in this text. It says Paul “was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.” (Acts 28:16) He stays by himself, and he has a soldier as a guard. Later we learn he has a rented house, but the text gives no name of anyone hosting him.

True. Paul tells them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.” (Acts 28:17) He opens by calling them brothers and telling them where he stands. Then he tells them how he ended up in chains.

The text says the opposite, friend. Paul tells the leaders, “…I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers…” (Acts 28:17). That's how he starts his explanation. Then he tells them he was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.

Yes. Paul says the Romans “examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) They looked into it and wanted him released. That's what Paul tells the leaders.

No island in that plan, baker. Paul says the Romans “wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) Paul has already been on one island, Malta (Acts 28:1), and that was the shipwreck, not the Romans' idea. What they wanted was to let him go.

Chains are where he ended up, but not what the Romans wanted. Paul says they “wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) The chain he mentions in verse 20 came after the Jews objected and he appealed to Caesar. So they wanted him free.

Not quite, baker. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar, “even though I have no charge to bring against my nation.” (Acts 28:19) He isn't in Rome to accuse anyone. Appealing was what he had to do after the Jews objected.

False is right. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar, “even though I have no charge to bring against my nation.” (Acts 28:19) He isn't bringing charges against anybody. He tells them he's here because the Jews objected and he was compelled to appeal.

explanations.answer: Because of the hope of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's what he tells them. “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” (Acts 28:20) He doesn't name any crime. He says the hope of Israel is the reason for the chain.

explanations.answer: Because he broke a Roman law
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He told them the Romans examined him and found “no basis for a death sentence against me.” (Acts 28:18) The reason he gives for the chain is, “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” (Acts 28:20)

Caesar is where he appealed to, baker, not who he spoke against. Paul says he was compelled to appeal to Caesar (Acts 28:19). The reason he gives for the chain is, “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.” (Acts 28:20)

They say it plainly: “…we consider your views worth hearing…” (Acts 28:22). The leaders tell Paul they've had no letters and no reports about him from Judea. So they're willing to listen to him themselves. Not a bad way to open a conversation.

They never ask him to leave, baker. The leaders say, “…we consider your views worth hearing…” (Acts 28:22). Then they set a day to meet with Paul, and many people came to where he was staying (Acts 28:23). That's the opposite of showing him the door.

The leaders actually say none came from Judea. “We have not received any letters about you from Judea…” (Acts 28:21). Then they tell Paul, “…we consider your views worth hearing…” (Acts 28:22). They want to hear it from him.

The leaders say the opposite. “…we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.” (Acts 28:22) It isn't welcomed everywhere. They've heard talk against it all over, and still they want to hear Paul out.

False is right. The leaders say, “…we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.” (Acts 28:22) They've heard people speaking against it, not welcoming it. Even so, they say Paul's views are worth hearing.

explanations.answer: The Law of Moses and the Prophets
explanations.explanation: That's right. Paul was “persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.” (Acts 28:23) He used Scripture, and he taught from morning to evening. It's a long day, and I think he knew his material.

explanations.answer: Letters from the church in Judea
explanations.explanation: No letters here, baker. The leaders said they hadn't received any letters about Paul from Judea (Acts 28:21). Paul was “persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.” (Acts 28:23)

Not Roman teachers, friend. The text says Paul was “persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.” (Acts 28:23) He taught about the kingdom of God from morning to evening. Every bit of it came from those Scriptures.

explanations.answer: Some are convinced and others refuse
explanations.explanation: That's what happened. “Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.” (Acts 28:24) It was a split, and they disagreed among themselves. Same message, same day, different answers.

explanations.answer: Every one of them believes him
explanations.explanation: If only, baker. The text says, “Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.” (Acts 28:24) Some believed and some didn't. Then they disagreed among themselves and started to leave.

explanations.answer: None of them will listen at all
explanations.explanation: Somebody was listening. “Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.” (Acts 28:24) So some believed, and others refused. Paul didn't talk to an empty room, friend.

That's the reason in Isaiah's words. “For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.” (Acts 28:27) A callous heart is a hardened one. The words say they have closed their eyes, too.

explanations.answer: No one has explained it to them
explanations.explanation: The words Paul quotes give a different reason. “For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.” (Acts 28:27) Explaining isn't mentioned at all. The reason given is their heart.

explanations.answer: The message is too hard to follow
explanations.explanation: The words don't say that, baker. They say, “For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.” (Acts 28:27) The reason is the heart. Nothing in those words says the message is too hard.

True. Isaiah's words say, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Acts 28:27) Seeing, hearing, understanding and turning come first. Then comes the healing.

It's true, friend. The words Paul quotes say, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” (Acts 28:27) The healing comes with seeing, hearing, understanding and turning. It's right there in the verse.

The Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish. Paul says, “Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” (Acts 28:28) That's a big announcement, and he says they will listen.

Not the Pharisees, baker. Paul says, “Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” (Acts 28:28) The Pharisees were a Jewish group, and Paul doesn't name them here. The word is Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish.

Priests don't come up in his final words. Paul says, “Be advised, therefore, that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” (Acts 28:28) Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. That's who he names.

explanations.answer: All who come to visit him
explanations.explanation: That's right. Paul stayed “in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him.” (Acts 28:30) All who came, with no list of who could knock. That's a welcome I'd be proud of.

explanations.answer: Only those who agree with him
explanations.explanation: Not just his agreeable guests. The text says he was “welcoming all who came to visit him.” (Acts 28:30) He didn't turn anyone away, baker. All means all.
The text doesn't mention any approval, friend. It says Paul was “welcoming all who came to visit him.” (Acts 28:30) He did have a soldier to guard him (Acts 28:16). But the verse says all who came.

Quite the opposite, baker. “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.” (Acts 28:31) Boldly and freely, with no keeping quiet. He did it the whole time he was in that rented house.

False is right. The text says, “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.” (Acts 28:31) He didn't hold back, even as a prisoner. Boldly and freely, that's how the story ends.
